correctness.rationale: For a fixed residue \(x\bmod n\), the congruence \(xy\equiv0\pmod n\) has exactly \(\gcd(x,n)\) solutions. Summing by gcd classes gives \(T(n)=n\sum_{e\mid n}\varphi(e)/e\), whose prime-power factors are \(p^{a-1}((a+1)p-a)\). The diagonal zero-product solutions satisfy \(x^2\equiv0\), giving \(S(n)=\prod p^{\lfloor a/2\rfloor}\) by CRT. Deleting those loops and halving gives the edge count. Since zero is universal, every remaining distinct nonedge is at distance two, so the Hosoya and Wiener formulas follow. An independent brute-force check for every \(2\le n\le100\) matched the edge, annihilator-sum, and square-zero counts; the bundled verifier extends this check further.
risks: The product formula is specific to \(\mathbb Z_n\); the general finite-ring annihilator identity need not factor without additional structure.

originality.rationale: The 2024 primary paper was inspected through its full PDF and explicitly ends by asking for higher prime powers, \(p^kq\), \(p^kq^h\), and square-free products with arbitrarily many primes. It treats only special families and does not give the annihilator-sum product formula. Searches under prime graph, zero-product graph, annihilator sum, and gcd terminology found no published all-\(n\) Wiener formula. The audited theorem therefore genuinely dominates the special cases and answers all four stated infinite-family questions.

value.rationale: A single multiplicative formula replacing several case-by-case distance calculations and closing four explicit infinite families is a natural complete classification for this graph invariant. The proof is elementary, but the source itself left precisely these extensions open; shortness does not make the uniform result valueless.
risks: The result is not a general classification for arbitrary finite commutative rings.
